title: House name sampler in cross-stitch
subtitle: A personalised house name with door and window motifs on 14-count Aida
excerpt: A house name sampler stitches the name of a house or address below a small pictorial house motif, a door, two windows, and a chimney, on 14-count Aida. The piece is 100-by-90 stitches and uses six floss colours. The house graphic is worked first; the name below uses a 7-stitch-tall block alphabet. Finished size is about 18 x 16 cm.
sourceNotes: Original design for Homemade cross-stitch library. House-name samplers are a persistent British domestic tradition documented in Royal School of Needlework publications and public collection samplers.

content.text: A house name sampler is a 100-by-90 stitch piece on 14-count

. The upper half holds a small pictorial house: a tiled roof, a coloured front door, two windows, and a chimney, all in full crosses. The lower half holds the house name or street address in a 7-stitch-tall block alphabet. Six
colours cover the house graphic; the name text uses one of those same colours so the piece reads as a unified design. A
line on the door and window outlines sharpens the architecture detail.

attrs.heading: Adapting for your house name
attrs.text: The name row accommodates up to fourteen letters at 7-stitch height with 1-stitch gaps. Short names (under seven letters) should be centred. House numbers are also supported, the digit alphabet is included in the chart. If the name has two words (e.g. 'Rose Cottage'), work both on the same row with a 3-stitch word gap, or split across two rows if the combined width exceeds fourteen characters.

items.name: 14-count Aida, cream
items.substitutions: Natural linen for a traditional aesthetic

items.name: DMC floss for house graphic
items.qty: 1 skein each: 321 (red tile/door), 3799 (dark outline), 3024 (pale walls), 3820 (warm yellow windows), 523 (garden greens), 3371 (door detail)

items.name: DMC floss for name text
items.substitutions: Any strong-contrast colour that matches the house graphic

content.text: Plan the name text letter spacing on the chart template before stitching anything. Count the total width and confirm it is narrower than the house graphic so the composition reads as house-above-name rather than name extending past the house.
Find the fabric centre and begin with the house door, the visual centre of the graphic section. Work outward to the walls, windows, roof, then the garden strip at the base.
Add the back-stitch outlines on the door and windows in 3799. These are worked after all the full-cross fills are complete.
Stitch the name from the centre letter outward in the row 6 stitches below the base of the house graphic.
Wash gently and press face-down. A mid-oak or dark-walnut frame with a cream mount suits the traditional sampler aesthetic. This is a good gift piece for a housewarming.

items.cause: The text was started from the left edge without first counting the total width of all letters plus gaps.
items.fix: Count the total stitch width of the name (letters plus one-stitch gaps between them) before threading. Divide by two to find the centre letter, and begin from the fabric centre. Once the centre letter is placed, count outward in both directions.

items.symptom: The number stitches look lighter than the letter stitches
items.cause: The number section was stitched with a different number of strands or a fresh skein from a different dye lot.
items.fix: Thread numbers and letters from the same skein and use the same strand count throughout. Check the dye lot number on the label before opening a second skein. If dye lots differ, stitch letters and numbers alternately from both skeins to blend the variation.

content.text: Once personalised samplers feel comfortable, try the be-kind small hoop or the gather quote piece. Both are quicker finishes that use a single word.

glossaryTerms.definition: A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads. The default for beginners. Counted in squares per inch: 11ct, 14ct, 16ct, and 18ct are the common counts.

The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch. Each skein is made of six strands twisted together loosely; the stitcher strips out the number of strands needed for the fabric count (two strands for 14-count Aida) and threads them together.

A solid outline stitch worked in a single strand along the back-stitch layer of the chart. You stitch backwards along the line one stitch at a time, each stitch finishing where the previous one started.
